a93.speaker: European Union (EU)
a93.speech: According to the EU, the Support Measures program is valued at US$7.3 million and consists of two key components. Said the Cooperation Facility aims to enhance the national aid development coordination mechanism to maximize the impact and effectiveness of EU-supported development programs by empowering various CSOs and NGOs and recognizing them as the backbone of a thriving democratic society. Said the Spotlight Initiative (2.0) program will be implemented by UN Women, UNFPA, and UNDP and is expected to be carried out in eight of Liberia's fifteen counties, including Bong, Grand Bassa, Cape Mount, Grand Gedeh, Lofa, Maryland, Montserrado, and Nimba.

a93.speaker: Erica Gerretsen, EU Director for Human Development, Migration, Governance and Peace
a93.speech: "So the signing of this financing agreement today is a signal that we are a reliable partner to Liberia that we are maintaining our commitment to gender equality and to fighting gender-based violence, but more broadly, a strong commitment from the EU to work with Liberia as a trusted partner and to continue reinforcing our relationship moving forward." ; Narrated that the first phase is a support measures program that will help the EU support Liberia in strengthening the coordination mechanisms to implement EU cooperation while also supporting the country's CSOs and civil society organizations. ; Noted that it will also contribute to increasing accountability as well as visibility of EU cooperation in Liberia. ; Noted that the European Union and its member states support Liberia on average by $100 million per year, with other EU countries involved including Ireland, Sweden, France, and Germany. ; Added that the second program signed was for a total of 13 million euros (approximately $14 million), saying "I would like to really thank and recognize the presence of the Minister of Gender this morning here in the room, as well as the UN system." ; Said the Spotlight Initiative is a worldwide initiative that the EU started with the UN system to fight gender-based violence around the world: "We had the first initiative, Spotlight One, which was launched back in 2017, for which Liberia has also been a beneficiary." "Violence against women and girls happens everywhere in every country; it's not something specific to Liberia; this is something that is happening everywhere in the world."

a93.speaker: Augustine K. Ngafuan, Liberia's Finance and Development Planning Minister
a93.speech: Termed the signing of the $20 million grant as a new day for the country, which is experiencing interesting times. Recalled that back in 2015, when the Sustainable Development Goals were agreed by the world, the central theme was "leave no one behind," and noted that this was the commitment of the world to look at the vulnerable, the poor, the weak, victims of gender-based violence, and to look at our daughters. "Leave no one behind. As I said on Friday, that concept of leaving no one behind is also a race because it has been left behind."

a301.speaker: Hon. Hawa Loleyah Norris, Superintendent of Bong County
a301.speech: Emphasized the importance of community consensus: "All that we agreed on here today, I want to ensure it is the decision of all the people in all the affected communities through their representatives here present"; assured citizens that their concerns and recommendations would be forwarded to the Bong County Legislative Caucus and the national government for consideration.

a301.speaker: Hon. Hawa Loleyah Norris, Superintendent of Bong County
a301.speech: Acknowledged the importance of making demands for community development but stressed that communities affected by ArcelorMittal Liberia's operations must recognize the value of the concession's presence and protect its investments: "While it is good to make demands, communities impacted by ArcelorMittal Liberia's operations need to embrace the operation of the concession and protect its investments."

a301.speaker: Hon. Hawa Loleyah Norris, Superintendent of Bong County
a301.speech: Highlighted the mounting economic challenges faced by the government and pointed out that concession agreements such as ArcelorMittal's are crucial in supporting social development initiatives, particularly in light of the USAID drawdown, which has impacted funding for various programs; "Development cannot come if we continue to fight among ourselves and tear each other down... We need to come together, to move the county and district forward so that we change the way our communities look."

a301.speaker: Petition of the rail-impacted communities of Bong County
a301.speech: Acknowledged AML's contributions to Liberia's economic growth, job creation, infrastructure development, education and healthcare, while highlighting challenges including insufficient employment for local residents, environmental hazards, damage to roads and infrastructure, and delays in compensation for property damage; proposed an increase in social development funds to match AML's expanded production, prioritization of local employment and skills training, a legally binding rail corridor development fund, improved environmental protection measures, expanded social infrastructure commitments, repairs to roads and bridges, adequate compensation for affected residents and enhanced safety along the rail corridor; "We appreciate your leadership and look forward to your support in ensuring that this agreement delivers tangible benefits to our communities."

a500.speaker: Marcus S. Wleh, Head of Sustainability and External Relations at ArcelorMittal Liberia
a500.speech: Spoke on behalf of all the awardees and expressed appreciation for the honor of receiving the awards: "For all the partners of Liberia who receive awards, we are honored to be identified as part of a winning environment. Without a healthy environment, it will be difficult for us to do the work we want to do and to pay the taxes we want to pay." ; "I would like to thank the honorable commissioner general and the minister of commerce, and everybody involved. It's not an easy task, and we thank you for your patience, as well as for not issuing fines but always trying to help as much as possible. Thank you."

a500.speaker: Dorbor Jallah, Head of the Liberia Revenue Authority (LRA)
a500.speech: Revealed plans by the LRA for continued technological advancements to streamline tax processes, including the introduction of electronic fiscal devices and the shift from a Goods and Services Tax (GST) to a Value Added Tax (VAT) system, and emphasized the importance of modernization to increase compliance and improve revenue collection: "We are digitizing, and that is what our focus is going to be on for the next couple of years. We want to automate most of our processes and make it seamless for everyone involved." ; "The goal is to give greater transparency, so when you make your sales or provide services, in real time, we will be able to get that data. When you make your filing, we will already know what to expect."

a500.speaker: Dorbor Jallah, Head of the Liberia Revenue Authority (LRA)
a500.speech: Encouraged taxpayers to embrace these changes for the benefit of national development: "For us to get to billions, we all have to work together. And when we get there, we will see the benefit. This is about sustainable development, and it's about the progress of our country."

a766.speaker: Bank of Namibia (BoN) determination)
a766.speech: In its latest determination, the Bank of Namibia (BoN) has told commercial banks to implement relief measures, including the restructuring of loans, granting of loan moratoriums, and emergency funding under preferential terms ; said the recently-issued Determination on Policy Changes in Response to Economic and Financial Stability Challenges is the result of the persistent drought countrywide and comes into force with immediate effect, and that the determination was issued following the declaration of a State of Emergency on account of drought by President Nangolo Mbumba in May this year ; “The determination was issued to provide credit-related drought relief policy measures to assist farmers and agricultural business owners who are experiencing financial difficulties because of the drought. It provides relief to agricultural clients who can demonstrate that they have been severely affected by the drought over the past few years…” ; “It is a reflection of the bank’s ongoing commitment to support the agricultural sector during these challenging times by ensuring that local farmers and agricultural businesses have the financial flexibility they need to navigate the drought crisis.”

a766.speaker: Experts (unnamed)
a766.speech: Many experts have made various key recommendations to government to improve food availability, which included providing drought-resistant seeds and modern agricultural training to communal farmers, increasing capacity-building initiatives for agricultural extension officers, and expanding hydroponic fodder production across all regions ; it has also been recommended that the government continues monitoring key factors such as staple commodity prices, inflation impacts, seasonal rainfall patterns and the potential effects of La Niña to mitigate the crisis and ensure timely and effective humanitarian assistance.

a1037.speaker: Commentary in Nature Reviews Microbiology led by Dr Monray Williams
a1037.speech: issues a stark warning: global complacency must end, and sub-Saharan Africa must be placed at the centre of the research agenda, or risk losing control of the HIV-1 epidemic.

a1037.speaker: Dr Monray Williams, researcher in the Biomedical and Molecular Metabolism Research Unit, North-West University (NWU), and co-authors
a1037.speech: argue that the research imbalance — with most studies focusing on subtype B while subtype C remains significantly understudied — undermines the development of effective treatments, vaccines, and, ultimately, a cure ; “We cannot end a global pandemic by studying just a fraction of its biology.”

a1037.speaker: Commentary in Nature Reviews Microbiology (the authors)
a1037.speech: warns that this neglect could prove disastrous if new variants arise with increased transmissibility or drug resistance, and proposes a bold corrective strategy named HARNESS, whose core is the principle of self-reliance: African countries must strengthen their own research capabilities by investing in local laboratories, biobanks, genomic surveillance systems and the training of future scientists; the paper also advocates deeper South–South collaboration and argues funding should reflect disease burden rather than the preferences of external donors.

a1037.speaker: Dr Monray Williams, North-West University (NWU)
a1037.speech: writes, on the effect of recent cuts to global health initiatives such as PEPFAR, “This is the moment for Africa to reclaim agency over its health future.”

a1387.speaker: Dr Muda Yusuf, Director/CEO, Centre For the Promotion Of Private Enterprise (CPPE)
a1387.speech: Analyses that the inception of the Trump administration in the United States has remarkably changed the dynamics of global trade, global economic outlook and geopolitical trajectory, with multi-dimensional implications for the Nigerian economy: immediate and remote consequences for energy prices, trade relations, economic diplomacy, macroeconomic stability, donor funding and capital flows. On energy prices, he argues the scenario of a weakening of crude oil prices in the near term is very high, so the crude oil price benchmark of $75 per barrel in the 2025 budget may not hold, impacting the outlook for government revenue and foreign exchange earnings; the upside is that energy prices - diesel, PMS, jet fuel and gas - would drop globally, transmitting fast because of the deregulated regime of the oil and gas sector.

a1387.speaker: Dr Muda Yusuf, Director/CEO, Centre For the Promotion Of Private Enterprise (CPPE)
a1387.speech: On global trade: says the Trump administration has demonstrated an unequivocal commitment to the ideology of economic nationalism, protectionism, deglobalisation, unilateralism and reciprocity, and fragmentation of the global economy, unleashing retaliatory trade policy actions from a number of countries. He states that AGOA faces the prospect of being terminated, although Nigeria has very little to show for the opportunities offered by AGOA, while the tariff war offers some opportunities for export and investment for Nigeria; there is the prospect of high inflation in the USA and thus possible imported inflation for Nigeria, and the trade war may trigger a disruption of global supply chains.

a1387.speaker: Dr Muda Yusuf, Director/CEO, Centre For the Promotion Of Private Enterprise (CPPE)
a1387.speech: On remittances, revenue and the exchange rate: says diaspora remittances may be affected by the current immigration policy of the Trump administration, given an estimated 500,000 diaspora Nigerians in the United States; heightened prospects of a drop in oil prices would negatively impact government revenue and foreign exchange earnings, with implications for the fiscal deficit, government debt and exchange rate; and the prospects of a strong dollar are very high, meaning a weaker naira, higher import costs and inflation, while US Federal Reserve tightening could result in capital flow reversals posing a risk to the naira exchange rate.

a1387.speaker: Dr Muda Yusuf, Director/CEO, Centre For the Promotion Of Private Enterprise (CPPE)
a1387.speech: On the suspension of USAID intervention: states the value of USAID intervention in Nigeria in 2023 was $1.02 billion, mainly in health, especially HIV/AIDS, water and sanitation, education, maternal and child care and disease prevention, as well as programmes to promote democracy and improve governance transparency. "The suspension and possible termination of the entire aid programme would create significant financing gaps for some government programmes, especially in the health sector. Thankfully, the relevant agencies of government are already taking steps to mitigate the steps possible consequences of the termination of USAID programs in these sectors."

a1387.speaker: Dr Muda Yusuf, Director/CEO, Centre For the Promotion Of Private Enterprise (CPPE)
a1387.speech: On policy implications and lessons: says there is a need for the government to commit more to the policy of self-reliance and less import dependence in critical areas of the economy, especially energy, food, pharmaceuticals and security, because excessive import dependence poses a major risk to economic and social security; a key lesson from the disruption is that no country should be too dependent on others for its strategic needs. He urges that supply chains be localised as much as possible, that domestic economic policies be framed within the reality of economic nationalism and deglobalisation, that the government deepen backward integration and export development, place special emphasis on food, energy, health and internal security, address productivity shortcomings in the real sector, and protect domestic industries against unfair competition from imports.

a1387.speaker: Trump administration
a1387.speech: Has committed to increasing oil output to reduce energy prices in the USA and globally; President Trump has signed an Executive Order creating a National Energy Dominance Council to drive the country's energy dominance agenda. Additionally, the Trump administration is committed to moderating the current global geopolitical tension, especially the Russian-Ukraine war, and possibly the Israeli Hamas war.

a1406.speaker: Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS)
a1406.speech: Issued a stark warning this week, predicting that 47 million people will face food insecurity within the next three months ; issued an alert this week warning that approximately 47 million people in the region will face a food crisis between June and August 2025 if no action is taken to address the current food security situation. According to the organisation, 34.7 million people in the region currently require immediate food and nutrition assistance.

a1406.speaker: One of the event's observers (anonymous)
a1406.speech: According to one of the event's observers, the region's food security challenges are exacerbated by the erratic nature of weather patterns, which is increasingly attributed to climate change.

a1406.speaker: Massandje Toure-Litse, ECOWAS Commissioner for Economic Affairs and Agriculture (represented by Mohammed Zongo, Acting Executive Director of ECOWAS Regional Agency for Agriculture and Food)
a1406.speech: Emphasised the importance of strengthening the region's immediate response mechanisms while laying the groundwork for long-term resilience. She stated that the food and nutrition security situation in West Africa and the Sahel has deteriorated significantly in recent years, and that the nutritional crisis persists in several areas of the region, with global acute malnutrition rates ranging between 10 and 14%: "Analyses conducted in December 2024, based on the Harmonised Framework, revealed that nearly 34.7 million people require immediate food and nutrition assistance. If appropriate measures are not implemented, this figure could rise to 47 million by the lean season of June to August 2025." ; "Furthermore, the nutritional crisis continues in several areas of our region, with global acute malnutrition rates ranging from 10% to 14%. Faced with this concerning situation, exacerbated by several challenges, including geopolitical reconfiguration of the region, persistent conflicts, economic crises, climate change, and chronic food insecurity, our region must strengthen its immediate response mechanisms while laying the groundwork for sustainable resilience." ; "Food security stocks appear to be key social protection tools, used at various scales-local, national, and regional-to respond effectively to food crises."

a1406.speaker: Massandje Toure-Litse, ECOWAS Commissioner for Economic Affairs and Agriculture
a1406.speech: Stated that the meeting "will allow us to take stock of the operations carried out by the Regional Reserve since March 2023 based on the Executive Board's guidelines, particularly in terms of purchases, interventions, stock replenishment, technical rotations, and the identification of new storage spaces." It will also allow us to plan operations for 2025, ensuring that Member States can care for the populations most affected by the food, nutritional, and pastoral crises. ; "Our discussions and decisions will ensure the Reserve's management is transparent, efficient, and fair, while also adapting to current and future challenges. As you are aware, for nearly ten years, our actions have been part of the regional storage strategy. We learnt a lot by comparing the theory of the regional storage strategy to its practical application on the ground." ; "We are also confronted with new challenges as the sociopolitical landscape in our region and around the world shifts. This is why we must adjust this strategy and the Regional Reserve's operating rules to improve the coordination and effectiveness of our collective action."

a1406.speaker: Senator Abubakar Kyari, Nigeria's Minister for Agriculture and Food Security (represented by Marcus Ogunbiyi, Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security)
a1406.speech: Stated that the food challenge serves as a reminder of the urgent need to strengthen strategies and response instruments to effectively address the region's food and nutrition crisis, and emphasised that the food reserve has become a critical component of the region's collective strategy for responding to the food and nutrition crisis. He stated, "This meeting is taking place at a particularly worrying time for our region; it is common knowledge globally, particularly in West Africa and the Sahel, that the food security situation has deteriorated in recent years as a result of conflicts, economic insecurity, and the devastating impact of climate change." A situation exacerbated by a drop in funding, geopolitical concerns in the region, and a general lack of food availability. ; "These major challenges highlight the urgent need to strengthen our strategies and response instruments to effectively address the food and nutrition crisis affecting our region. They also highlight the growing need for sovereign financing of our agriculture in general, as well as our food crisis response mechanisms." ; "This, therefore, calls for a deliberate concerted effort to address food production, strategic food storage, markets, and price volatility, as well as re-strategizing of the regional body, particularly in the administration and management of the regional food security reserve."

a1406.speaker: Cadre Harmonise report (December 2024)
a1406.speech: According to the most recent cadre Harmonise report (December 2024), nearly 34.7 million people require immediate food and nutritional assistance.

a1502.speaker: Dambisa Moyo, Zambian author (book, Dead Aid)
a1502.speech: argues that millions are actually poorer because of aid, unable to escape corruption and reduced, in the West's eyes, to a childlike state of beggary.

a1502.speaker: Siobhan Walsh, CEO of Ireland's GOAL Global
a1502.speech: argues aid is working if it is applied to its intended purpose: "We can't say aid is not working at all, I have seen it when it changes the lives of youth to thrive." ; "There is a lot of argument about Aid but what I would say is if aid is delivered effectively and it's how it is done is very important... if aid is addressing a problem and if it is done in consultation with communities or with local organizations for me that is the most effective way. We have seen in these and in many other countries how aid can help and not just to survive but thrive. If you work on the longer term problem and the root causes sustain what you are doing you absolutely can transform people's lives. There is an argument about aid not working but I have seen that aid is working if it is done properly and in a sustainable way."

a1502.speaker: Siobhan Walsh, CEO of Ireland's GOAL Global
a1502.speech: On GOAL's work and funding: "We have been here since 1984 and are working in many different sectors. The core sectors we work on: water, shelter; are emergency services we provide. We also work with refugees and internally displaced people; helping them with food, non-food items, health, food security and livelihoods. To do this job we get money from USAID, Irish Aid, UNOCHA, UK and ECHO but we also have a lot of funding from private foundations and from the public. In Ireland, we depend on the Irish people to support Goal's work. We have a diversity of funds. In Ethiopia we work in Gambela, Afar, Oromia, west Gedio, Addis Ababa and Hawassa."

a1502.speaker: Siobhan Walsh, CEO of Ireland's GOAL Global
a1502.speech: On GOAL's five-year strategic plans: "We are known for our work. We respond well to people who are suffering in times of crisis and we will continue that. We also want to focus on youth... we need to assist them. We need to work on food, livelihood, health and nutrition since they are the core areas of Goal and over the next three years we will continue to do that with direct delivery and through partnership with another organization."

a1502.speaker: Siobhan Walsh, CEO of Ireland's GOAL Global
a1502.speech: On overlapping NGO work: "That is not unique to Ethiopia and to be honest a lot work has to be done with coordination. The UN also has to play a role with that and the government in terms of conversations about whose is what and who should do what where and I think all the NGOs should work on this issue. We need a constant conversation with the UN and other stakeholders to avoid overlapping work."

a1502.speaker: Siobhan Walsh, CEO of Ireland's GOAL Global
a1502.speech: On responding to Ethiopia's humanitarian crisis: "I think Goal takes what I would call a pragmatic approach for example with the influx of refugees from Eretria in the north east. Goal will assess the situation and see what is needed because if you have the influx of refugees, it impacts the local communities. Working with the local government to agree on that what we have done is food and water... it is not just dealing with the issue of the malnourished child but is the longer term it is about food and it is about how you keep your child healthy. We also working on shelter because shelter is big issue and a big problem and we are doing that in consultation with the government locally. We are also sending outreach workers into the community to ensure that local people are also identified."

a1502.speaker: Siobhan Walsh, CEO of Ireland's GOAL Global
a1502.speech: On the meeting between Irish and Ethiopian leaders: "We got the chance to meet with the Irish PM. In fact, all the Irish NGOs met with him and we talked about what each of the agencies were doing... he met with the Ethiopian PM, another young leader and they talked about a unique partnership between the two countries... They announced a tourism partnership between them... The message we gave to our PM is to continue supporting and investing in Ethiopia because our evidence over the year is that investment in development is working and we need to continue that sustained support and we need to make sure that the government is committed. The Irish government has very bold strategy for 2025 to do more development work and by coming here in Ethiopia he was deepening that commitment."

a1502.speaker: Siobhan Walsh, CEO of Ireland's GOAL Global
a1502.speech: On refugees: "Refugees are a reality of every country. Most refugees want to return home... I actually think the Ethiopian government has also demonstrated a lot of courage and leadership by having an open door policy towards refugees because they have over 800,000 refugees and that shows tremendous leadership as a country to be so accepting of people in real need. There is no easy answer for this question. Countries and leaders and governments across the world are dealing with migration. This will change countries in the future so it is an ongoing conversation across the world." ; On fears about refugees: "It is understandable that there is a creation of fear about how it will change culture and shift society when you have big influx of refugees into your country. Even in Europe there is a lot of debate about how refugees will change culture and identity. If you look at the US, it is a melting pot of every nationality across the world and you see the strength of diversity and you see the creation of business and how it is good for the economy in the longer term. So for me there is not just one answer to this question."

a1502.speaker: Siobhan Walsh, CEO of Ireland's GOAL Global
a1502.speech: On GOAL's finances: "Our budget for this year is over USD 100 million. Every year our budget depends on how many emergencies we respond to. There is a plan for each country. For example, Goal Ethiopia's budget is USD 12 million and with this plan on our table we will go to our donors and ask to partner with us. We are also working with the public and corporate services to raise more money."

a1502.speaker: Siobhan Walsh, CEO of Ireland's GOAL Global
a1502.speech: On the challenges facing international NGOs: "The ever changing context in which we work. Conflict areas are the big concern for us. Places like Syria with protracted crisis. Making sure we have sustained commitment and other challenges like trying to build capacity and trying to find key partners, migration and climate change are shaping NGOs."

a1502.speaker: Siobhan Walsh, CEO of Ireland's GOAL Global
a1502.speech: On the past staff procurement corruption scandal and internal controls: "You are going back three years now which is before I came to the organization... when I look at the organization now, the strengthening systems of Goal are very strong. To be honest with you, many other organizations have come to asked to look at the Goal system which to me is a testament to the strength of how Goal manages and operates. The workers are very tight and the field team sometimes complains about how tight they are but that is for a good reason. For me coming into the organization as a new CEO I am very confident that the organization has good transparency, accountability and my responsibility is to make sure our good work is sustaining and to make sure of our accountability to the people and donors we work with."

a1518.speaker: Transparency International
a1518.speech: Consistently ranks Somalia among the most corrupt countries globally.

a1538.speaker: Lazarus Chakwera, President of Malawi
a1538.speech: Conceded defeat in the 16 September general elections and congratulated his successor, opposition figure Peter Mutharika of the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP); speaking from Lilongwe, he called for national unity and for all citizens to rally behind the president-elect.

a1538.speaker: Malawi Council of Churches (MCC) and former president Bakili Muluzi
a1538.speech: Encouraged the concession, aimed at guaranteeing a peaceful transition.

a1538.speaker: Malawi Electoral Commission (MEC)
a1538.speech: Credits Mutharika with 66% of the vote against 24% for Chakwera, pending the official proclamation of the final results.

a1634.speaker: Southern African Development Community (SADC) communique
a1634.speech: In a communique issued after eight Southern African Development Community heads of state met virtually, the regional organisation noted that El Nino had caused drought and floods across Southern Africa affecting 61 million people.

a1820.speaker: Selma Ashipala-Musavyi, Namibian Minister of International Relations and Trade
a1820.speech: Says Namibia is placing particular focus on exploring cooperation in nuclear energy with its bilateral partners, and that the decision to add nuclear energy to its energy mix is part of the country's infrastructural development and in line with the Swapo Party Manifesto. "Such partnerships are expected to encompass multiple dimensions of nuclear cooperation, including nuclear power plant development, training programmes for capacity building, joint research initiatives on advanced nuclear fuels, and investment in specialised mining and processing infrastructure. This also represents a key component of the Sixth National Development Plan (NDP6), which prioritises domestic processing capabilities of mineral resources, technology transfer and industrial diversification."

a1820.speaker: Selma Ashipala-Musavyi, Namibian Minister of International Relations and Trade
a1820.speech: Highlights that the eighth administration has placed living standards and sustained prosperity at the centre of government priorities, with areas such as agriculture, sports, youth empowerment, quality education and health, creative industries and others identified to drive growth. "Increasingly and in line with the Sustainable Development Goals, we are all placing the welfare of our people at the centre of our work by optimising economic diplomacy. Namibia is no different, and this in most part informed the decision of Her Excellency Dr Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah, President of the Republic of Namibia, to merge the portfolios of International Relations, Trade and Investment. This was also to ensure better coordinated synergies in the pursuit of our economic diplomacy, while at the same time promoting regional and continental economic integration and enhancing opportunities offered by the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA)."

a1820.speaker: Selma Ashipala-Musavyi, Namibian Minister of International Relations and Trade
a1820.speech: Announces that the Ministry will introduce regional diplomatic outreach with the aim of exploring the cultural diversity and the economic competitiveness of each region.

a1820.speaker: The diplomatic corps
a1820.speech: Propose regular group consultations, labelling the priorities under NDP6 as mutually beneficial for Namibia and their respective countries.

a2192.speaker: Victoria Shimwandi, beneficiary of the programme
a2192.speech: Said the food has been of great help in her life, as she no longer worries about purchasing maize meal: "It really helped me a lot. I no longer struggle for maize. With the little I have I buy relish" ; said the food sustains her daughter and grandchild.

a2192.speaker: Jessica Long, deputy chief of mission (US Embassy)
a2192.speech: Speaking at the handover of the food donation, said Namibia vulnerability assessment committee already in 2019 indicated that 42% of households were already severely food insecure; said the assessment suggested a significant increase in the number of people in need of urgent action to protect their livelihoods and increase food access; said the situation is further exacerbated by natural disasters such as drought and pandemics such as Covid-19, which have further increased household vulnerability ; "We know that years of drought have left families and communities in dire straits and that the effects of Covid-19 on the economy have further exasperated the situation by leaving many people unemployed."

a2192.speaker: Jessica Long, deputy chief of mission (US Embassy)
a2192.speech: On the HIV front, said the country is close to reaching the 95-95-95 milestone ; "So access to food leads to a reduction in morbidity and mortality among people living with HIV."

a2192.speaker: Jessica Long, deputy chief of mission (US Embassy)
a2192.speech: Further stressed that with the food vouchers, communities can now support local retailers and cut on transportation cost, leaving more money for the needy families.

a2192.speaker: Namibia Vulnerability Assessment Committee (2019 assessment)
a2192.speech: Indicated that 42% of households were already severely food insecure, and suggested a significant increase in the number of people in need of urgent action to protect their livelihoods and increase food access.

a2209.speaker: US Supreme Court (5-4 decision)
a2209.speech: Declined to let President Donald Trump's administration withhold payment to foreign aid organisations for work they already performed for the government, upholding in a 5-4 decision Washington-based US District Judge Amir Ali's order that had called on the administration to promptly release funding to contractors and recipients of grants from USAID and the State Department for their past work.

a2209.speaker: Amir Ali, US District Judge (Washington-based)
a2209.speech: Ordered that the Trump administration promptly release funding to contractors and recipients of grants from USAID and the State Department for their past work, originally giving the administration until 26 February to disburse the funding; his 25 February enforcement order applied to payment for work done by foreign aid groups before 13 February, when he issued his temporary restraining order to prevent irreparable harm to the plaintiffs while he considers their claims.

a2209.speaker: Conservative Justices Samuel Alito, Clarence Thomas, Neil Gorsuch and Brett Kavanaugh
John Roberts, Chief Justice of the US Supreme Court
a2209.speech: Paused Judge Ali's order hours before the midnight deadline to give the Supreme Court additional time to consider the administration's more formal request to block Ali's ruling.

a2209.speaker: Sarah Harris, Acting Solicitor General
a2209.speech: Said in a Supreme Court filing on 3 March that blocking Ali's order "is warranted to prevent reinstatement of a new, short-fused deadline that would unlawfully commandeer federal payment processes anew"; argued that the judge's order amounted to judicial overreach and had given the administration too little time to scrutinise the invoices "to ensure the legitimacy of all payments".

a2209.speaker: Lawyers representing the Trump administration
a2209.speech: Said in a separate 26 February filing that full payments could take weeks.

a2209.speaker: Aid organisations (plaintiffs, including the AIDS Vaccine Advocacy Coalition, Journalism Development Network, DAI Global and HIAS)
a2209.speech: Accused Trump in lawsuits of exceeding his authority under federal law and the US Constitution by effectively dismantling an independent federal agency and canceling spending authorised by Congress; said in a Supreme Court filing on 28 February that they "would face extraordinary and irreversible harm if the funding freeze continues," as would their employees and those who depend on their work; said their "work advances US interests abroad and improves - and, in many cases, literally saves - the lives of millions of people across the globe" ; "The government's actions have largely brought this work to a halt," the lawyers wrote, adding that the Trump administration "comes to this court with an emergency of its own making".

a2209.speaker: Global aid groups
a2209.speech: Have said the US retreat endangers the lives of millions of the world's most vulnerable people, including those facing deadly diseases and those living in conflict zones.

a2209.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a2209.speech: Has called his agenda an "America First" agenda, and ordered a 90-day pause on all foreign aid on his first day back in office on 20 January.

a2316.speaker: Africa Command of the United States Armed Forces (AFRICOM)
a2316.speech: reported that the United States has completely finished the withdrawal of its troops from Niger.

a2316.speaker: US Department of Defense and Ministry of Defense of the Republic of Niger (joint statement)
a2316.speech: "The US Department of Defense and the Ministry of Defense of the Republic of Niger have announced the finalisation of the withdrawal of American military personnel and assets from Niger," the statement says ; it is also noted that the withdrawal of American troops proved to be "safe, orderly and responsible", thanks to effective interaction and communication between the United States and the military in Niger.

a2335.speaker: Elon Musk, billionaire adviser to US President Donald Trump
a2335.speech: Last week said he was working to shut down the world's largest international development agency, which disbursed $43.8 billion globally in 2023.

a2335.speaker: US Department of State
a2335.speech: According to the US Department of State, the US government was giving more than $350m to Malawi annually, representing more than 13 percent of the 2024/25 Budget of the recipient country.

a2335.speaker: Unicef
a2335.speech: According to Unicef, between 2019 and 2023 foreign donations accounted for 11 percent of the education budget and 80 percent of spending on capital projects such as schools, with USAid accounting for a quarter of this.

a2335.speaker: Moses Kunkuyu, Malawi's Minister of Information and Digitalisation
a2335.speech: "Developed countries like the US know and appreciate that Malawi is one country that has invested heavily in efforts to eradicate poverty, disease and other socioeconomic ills" ; "But, being a repetitive victim of natural disasters and global economic woes, it is clear that Malawi still needs a hand."

a2335.speaker: Pemphero Mphamba, health economics researcher, Kamuzu University of Health Sciences
a2335.speech: "Malawi is already experiencing some devastating consequences" ; She said the economy's dire state could worsen, with high inflation estimated above 23 percent since June 2022 following steep currency devaluations amid foreign exchange shortages ; "USAid was another source of forex."

a2335.speaker: International Monetary Fund
a2335.speech: According to the International Monetary Fund, last year Malawi's GDP per capita was just $481.

a2335.speaker: World Bank
a2335.speech: Estimates that for the past three years the economy has been growing slower than the population, now estimated at over 21 million ; according to the World Bank, the country exported just $900 million of goods in 2022, of which tobacco totalled 40 percent.

a2335.speaker: Victor Chipofya, political scientist, Blantyre International University
a2335.speech: "As a country, we have been relying on one source of revenue collection for the longest time and that's tobacco. So how does a country sustain itself with a product that globally everybody is campaigning against?" ; He estimated several thousand people were working for NGOs and projects funded by USAid ; "These were middle-class employees and obviously they were spending and they were able to pay taxes. As a country, we were benefitting from that … and now these people are unemployed."

a2335.speaker: Yvonne Mhango, Africa economist at Bloomberg
a2335.speech: Said the sudden withdrawal of US support could undo some of the aid-related gains Malawi has made, and that the end of aid dependency was not in sight either ; "I don't think that will happen for a generation… It's not like it's got a vibrant stock exchange or debt market or foreign direct investment coming in in a big way because they don't have a consumer market."

a2335.speaker: Christopher Vandome, Chatham House research fellow
a2335.speech: Said there were valid criticisms of aid for not catalysing sustainable, long-term growth ; "But the immediate reality is that government spending and so many of the government's social provisions are dependent upon that donor support."

a2398.speaker: Enock Mponda, KCM Acting Chief Executive Officer
a2398.speech: Says the MoU is key to fulfilling important steps of post-employment life as it would allow workers to access agricultural equipment such as tractors, ploughs, disc harrows, planters, boom sprayers and many more while they were still in employment ; said many Zambians are joining government’s push to make the country a major agricultural producer of export crops and livestock while remaining food sufficient, and hoped that KCM employees would take advantage of the collaboration with CAMCO to ensure they secure their future ; “This occasion will linger in our minds for a very long time to come because of the nature and magnitude of the collaboration that KCM and CAMCO are signing for. It is evident that every person has an after-life from the professional jobs we do and agriculture offers a lot of opportunities for that period when we shall all detach ourselves from mining, in the case of KCM employees.”

a2398.speaker: Bernard Chiwala, CAMCO Marketing Director
a2398.speech: Said the company aims to fill the mechanisation and value addition gap that exists within small and medium scale farming ; said the opportunity to work with KCM workers would widen the market for CAMCO equipment and other services ; “We look forward with pleasure to working with KCM management and staff as we embark on the journey to transform lives through farming. The participation of more people such as your employees in agricultural activities will help cushion the maize shortage and will largely contribute to the Gross Domestic Product of the Country.”

a2522.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a2522.speech: took office vowing an “America First” policy of tightly restricting assistance overseas.

a2522.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State (internal memo to staff seen by AFP)
a2522.speech: “No new funds shall be obligated for new awards or extensions of existing awards until each proposed new award or extension has been reviewed and approved,” said the memo to staff ; the memo explicitly made exceptions for military assistance to Israel and Egypt, and Rubio also made an exception for US contributions to emergency food assistance; the memo allows the State Department to make other case-by-case exceptions and temporarily to fund salaries to staff and other administrative expenses, and called for an internal review of all foreign assistance within 85 days ; In justifying the freeze, Rubio wrote that it was impossible for the new administration to assess whether existing foreign aid commitments “are not duplicated, are effective and are consistent with President Trump's foreign policy.”

a2522.speaker: Lawmakers from the rival Democratic Party
a2522.speech: said that more than 20 million people relied on medication through PEPFAR and 63 million people on US-funded anti-malaria efforts including nets.

a2522.speaker: Representative Gregory Meeks, top Democrat on the House Foreign Relations Committee, and Representative Lois Frankel (letter)
a2522.speech: “For years, Republicans in Congress have decried what they see as a lack of U.S. credibility vis-a-vis countries like China, Russia, and Iran” ; “Now our credibility is on the line, and it appears we will cut and run from American commitments to our partners around the world,” they wrote in a letter ; Meeks and Frankel also noted that foreign assistance is appropriated by Congress and said they would seek its implementation.

a2522.speaker: Oxfam (anti-poverty group)
a2522.speech: said that Trump was abandoning a longstanding consensus in the United States for foreign assistance.

a2522.speaker: Abby Maxman, Oxfam America president (statement)
a2522.speech: “Humanitarian and development assistance accounts for only around one percent of the federal budget; it saves lives, fights diseases, educates millions of children and reduces poverty” ; “Suspending and ultimately cutting many of these programs could have life or death consequences for countless children and families who are living through crisis.”

a2522.speaker: Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD)
a2522.speech: According to the OECD, the United States gave more than $64 billion in overseas development assistance in 2023, the last year for which records were available.

a2539.speaker: Zimbabwe Anti-Corruption Commission (ZACC)
a2539.speech: Has said it had recorded 150 corruption cases at the Beitbridge border post in the last four years, mainly collusion between customs clearing agents and Zimbabwe Revenue Authority (Zimra) officials in the form of smuggling and under-invoicing goods for personal gain. Of all the cases received, 65 individuals were arrested while some are already serving jail term.

a2539.speaker: Michael Reza, ZACC chairperson
a2539.speech: Revealed the statistics at the 19th Shipping and Forwarding Agents Association of Zimbabwe (SFAAZ) conference held in Bulawayo. "A total of 150 cases were reported at Beitbridge border post alone where these syndicates have operated with impunity, we are actively pursuing those cases," he said ; "We have documented cases where corrupt officers conspired with clearing agents to undervalue goods, misclassify imports, and expedite illegal clearances for bribes," he said.

a2539.speaker: Michael Reza, ZACC chairperson
a2539.speech: Warned syndicates facilitating the smuggling of goods into the country that their days are numbered, saying government will show no mercy to those treating border posts as hubs for illicit enrichment. "There will be no mercy for those who treat our borders as a playground for illicit enrichment. Please take a firm stand against corruption. Adopt integrity pledges." ; He said lawlessness stifles socio economic progress and will not be tolerated.

a2539.speaker: Michael Reza, ZACC chairperson
a2539.speech: Acknowledged customs agents' critical role in driving Zimbabwe's economic growth and realisation of the country's development aspirations, but expressed deep concern over rampant corruption within the sector. "I am told that SFAAZ members handle over 95 percent of the country's commercial imports and exports. This means that you play a crucial role in the revenue collection, and therefore, it is important for your membership to uphold integrity. It is a point of bother that there is rampant and systemic corruption within your sector. SFAAZ members have, or let me say, some SFAAZ members have become conduits for smuggling, under-invoicing," said Reza ; "Recent investigations have exposed shocking cases, where members of your association facilitated fraud. We have in the past arrested clearing agents and importers for smuggling thousands of tissues and suitcases disguised as agricultural equipment."

a2635.speaker: Antoine Gerard, UN deputy humanitarian co-ordinator for Sudan
a2635.speech: Told the BBC that a landslide has killed at least 370 people in the remote Marra Mountains in western Sudan, and said that it was hard to assess the scale of the incident or the exact death toll as the area was very hard to reach ; Said getting aid quickly to the area would be difficult: “We do not have helicopters, everything goes in vehicles on very bumpy roads. It takes time and it is the rainy season - sometimes we have to wait hours, maybe a day or two to cross a valley... bringing in trucks with commodities will be a challenge.”

a2635.speaker: Sudan Liberation Movement/Army (statement)
a2635.speech: Had earlier said that at least 1,000 people had died, and said in a statement that days of heavy rain triggered the landslide on Sunday, which left just one survivor and “levelled” much of the village of Tarseen ; The movement has appealed for humanitarian assistance from the UN and other regional and international organisations.

a2635.speaker: Minni Minnawi, Darfur's army-aligned governor
a2635.speech: Called the landslide a “humanitarian tragedy”: “We appeal to international humanitarian organisations to urgently intervene and provide support and assistance at this critical moment, for the tragedy is greater than what our people can bear alone,” he said in a statement quoted by the AFP news agency.

a2635.speaker: US official (anonymous)
a2635.speech: Last year estimated up to 150,000 people had been killed since hostilities began in 2023.

a2646.speaker: Nigerian Catholic Priests Association (NCPA), Makurdi Diocese
a2646.speech: Has called on the Federal and Benue governments to take decisive actions to end continuous killings in the state.

a2646.speaker: Rev. Fr Joseph Beba, NCPA Chairman, Makurdi Diocese
a2646.speech: Addressing newsmen on Sunday in Makurdi, condemned the recent gruesome attacks on their brothers and sisters, including Rev. Fr Solomon Atongo, and said the coordinated violence unleashed on the communities of Tse Orbiam, Ahume, Jimba, Nagi-Camp, Aondoana, Yelewata and Abegana within one month has left more than 50 people dead, including women and children ; Described the acts as inhumane, barbaric, and a gross violation of the sanctity and dignity of human life.

a2646.speaker: Rev. Fr Joseph Beba, NCPA Chairman, Makurdi Diocese (on security agencies)
a2646.speech: Urged the security agencies, especially the military, to be consciously and deliberately professional and patriotic in the discharge of their duties across Nigeria, and further urged them that the same level of efficiency, swiftness and vigilance they often display during general elections must be applied to protecting lives and communities in Benue and across Nigeria.

a2646.speaker: Rev. Fr Joseph Beba, NCPA Chairman, Makurdi Diocese (on government responsibility)
a2646.speech: “Government must be responsible and accountable and must respond by action and not only by mere press statements in the comfort of their conference rooms and offices. We remind both the federal and state governments of their constitutional mandate to safeguard the lives and dignity of all citizens. This is a sacred duty they swore to, and this must be pursued with urgency, sincerity, and transparency. We request immediate compensation to victims of this violence and the return of those displaced to their ancestral homes. We call on the youth to be prepared to defend their faith, their farmlands and their way of life. The right to self-defence is an inalienable one for all citizens,” he said ; Reminded the state and federal governments of their responsibility to provide water, housing, education, freedom of worship and security against all evil men and women.

a2646.speaker: Rev. Fr Joseph Beba, NCPA Chairman, Makurdi Diocese (on the church's role)
a2646.speech: Said the association was firmly committed to the truth of the gospel and shall do everything possible and necessary within the ambit of the law to resist any form of intimidation and threats to silence those speaking truth to power ; According to him, the church of Makurdi Diocese has always provided material and humanitarian assistance to victims of these attacks, but the church has not been appreciated enough.

a2682.speaker: Ben M’bwana, Director of Administration at the Ministry of Gender, Community Development and Social Welfare
a2682.speech: Hailed the challenge, saying bicycles can have positive impact when it comes to economic empowerment, improved health outcomes and education access in Malawi. “Bicycles are not just a means of transport; they are a transformative tool for development and empowerment. In Sub-Saharan Africa, where over 78% of the population relies on walking to access work and essential services, bicycles can significantly enhance mobility and economic opportunities,” he said.

a2711.speaker: Jay Z (Shawn Carter), rapper, through his court filing
a2711.speech: claims that his accuser [Jane Doe] has not stopped making defamatory statements about him even though she had agreed to do so, and that those statements have cost him and his company Roc Nation millions of dollars ; claims that on April 11, Doe posted a video on TikTok aimed at misleading viewers into believing that Jay Z had tried to pay her a large sum of money so that she would apologise over the charges she had earlier filed against him.

a2711.speaker: Jay Z's lawyers
a2711.speech: filed a case in Alabama this week claiming their client was tarnished by the allegations.

a2711.speaker: Jane Doe, 37, plaintiff
a2711.speech: sued Jay Z and Diddy in October 2024 alleging that in 2000, when she was a 13-year-old girl, the artists raped her right after the MTV VMAs awards ceremony.

a2711.speaker: Alex Spiro, Jay Z's lawyer
a2711.speech: "The false case against Jay Z, which should never have been heard, has been thrown out." ; "By standing firm against false allegations, Jay Z has achieved what many have failed to do. He has not backed down nor paid a single cent to clear his name."

a2711.speaker: Rolling Stone
a2711.speech: has obtained Jay Z's complaint, which explains why Doe's actions are harming his business by causing the loss of many commercial opportunities.

a2711.speaker: Jay Z's complaint (court filing)
a2711.speech: "As a result of the defendants filing a false case and making other false statements to the public against Mr. Carter [Jay Z], they caused him to lose the opportunity to obtain a personal loan of $55 million. Roc Nation was also denied a $115 million loan."

a2711.speaker: Jay Z, through Roc Nation
a2711.speech: denied the allegations and said that he is not like other famous people, that he has been protecting children, and called the allegations ridiculous and aimed at obtaining some kind of benefit such as money.

a2711.speaker: Soulja Boy, rapper
a2711.speech: criticised what he called efforts to destroy the mark set publicly by famous rap figures, saying he is not prepared to see them pushed backwards by such things: "When you are in this industry and stand as a business they will start to tarnish your name, they will try to bring you down, they don't want to see us winning and they don't want to see us having this money. When you are in this rap industry and become a celebrity, you will simply be targeted."

a2906.speaker: Afrobarometer (ninth round survey, supported by USAID)
a2906.speech: Disclosed that it has been conducting its ninth round survey in Ethiopia with the support of the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), based on face-to-face interviews with a sample of some 2,400 citizens ; reported that the government's performance is very poor on stabilising prices (85 percent of respondents), on narrowing the gap between rich and poor (82 percent called the measures terrible), on job creation (74 percent said very poor) and on improving the lives of low-income citizens (73 percent said terrible), and that 56 percent of respondents believe the country is going in the wrong direction ; said citizens are dissatisfied with the country's overall direction, economic conditions and way of life, that most Ethiopians criticise the government's performance on key economic issues, and that properly managing the economy should be the government's first priority.

a2906.speaker: Study participants / respondents to the Afrobarometer survey
a2906.speech: Stated that the issue the government must address as its first priority is managing the economy properly, with 27 percent urging work on water supply, 23 percent on infrastructure construction, and others on easing internal and political conflicts.

a2906.speaker: Afrobarometer (climate change study presented last week)
a2906.speech: Presented that four out of ten Ethiopians say drought has worsened in their area over the past ten years, that three out of ten respondents (30 percent) had been exposed to severe flooding — 79 percent in Addis Ababa — and that fewer than half of Ethiopians have awareness about the climate despite repeated impacts on their livelihoods and safety, a lack of awareness that affects the provision of an appropriate early disaster response.

a3006.speaker: Diplomatic sources (anonymous)
a3006.speech: Described the meeting as one of the most significant moments in Mozambique's foreign policy in recent years; said that JD Vance assuming the role of number one in the American political hierarchy at that moment reflects the value the United States attaches to its relationship with Mozambique and to the country's role as an actor of stability and development in Southern Africa.

a3006.speaker: Observers in Washington (anonymous)
a3006.speech: "The meeting with JD Vance was a gesture of great political weight," not only because it took place at the White House, but because the Vice-President represented President Donald Trump, who was out of the country on an official mission on the Asian continent.

a3006.speaker: Daniel Francisco Chapo, President of the Republic of Mozambique
a3006.speech: Stressed that Mozambique is committed to "creating an attractive and predictable environment for foreign investment," and that the country is "opening a new era of economic cooperation," based on concrete results and transparency; underlined that the Government's objective is to transform the country's economic potential into real and sustainable development ; "We want a balanced partnership, one that is not based only on aid, but on productive investment, innovation and knowledge transfer."

a3006.speaker: Daniel Francisco Chapo, President of the Republic of Mozambique
a3006.speech: Explained that the country is diversifying its economy and betting heavily on industrialisation, the modernisation of agriculture and the expansion of the energy sector, including natural gas, solar and hydro projects; stressed that Mozambique wants to position itself as "a strategic supplier of clean energy" for the Southern African region, contributing at the same time to reducing the energy dependence of neighbouring countries.

a3006.speaker: Daniel Francisco Chapo, President of the Republic of Mozambique
a3006.speech: Reiterated the importance of Mozambique being seen as "a pillar of peace and security" in the region, reinforcing the country's commitment to dialogue and international cooperation; underlined the need for international partners to invest not only in large-scale projects, but also in capacity-building initiatives, technological innovation and youth training.

a3006.speaker: Daniel Francisco Chapo, President of the Republic of Mozambique
a3006.speech: At the end of the audience reaffirmed Mozambique's commitment to "working with all partners who believe in shared development and sustainable progress"; said the way forward involves "investing in people, in innovation and in good governance, because growth is only real when it improves people's lives."

a3006.speaker: JD Vance, Vice-President of the United States of America
a3006.speech: Praised the path of stability and reform that Mozambique has been consolidating; recognised "the remarkable advances" in the areas of economic governance and public finance management, underlining that the United States sees in Mozambique "a reliable partner with a vision for the future"; stated that the American Administration is available to "deepen economic relations and support structuring projects that create jobs and drive sustainable growth."

a3006.speaker: JD Vance, Vice-President of the United States of America
a3006.speech: Highlighted the interest of the US in strengthening cooperation in the field of energy, above all in energy transition projects and infrastructure modernisation ; "Mozambique is a country with vast potential, with sun, water and gas. We believe it can be a central actor in Africa's energy transformation and we are ready to support that path."

a3006.speaker: JD Vance, Vice-President of the United States of America
a3006.speech: Showed himself particularly interested in Mozambican policies of technical capacity-building and digitalisation of the State; highlighted the importance of training national cadres capable of managing and sustaining foreign investments, pointing to Mozambique as an example of a country aligning economic growth with social responsibility ; "What we see in Mozambique is a model of development that gives priority to people, education and environmental balance."

a3006.speaker: JD Vance, Vice-President of the United States of America
a3006.speech: On taking his leave, stressed that the meeting "reinforces mutual trust and opens space for joint projects in strategic sectors"; underlined that "the United States values Mozambique not only for its resources, but for its vision and stability."

a3006.speaker: Analysts consulted by O Pais
a3006.speech: Underline that this meeting "is the culmination of a series of diplomatic interactions that Mozambique has been developing with American institutions, including the IMF, the World Bank, the DFC and the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC)."

a3006.speaker: Sources close to the White House (anonymous)
a3006.speech: Consider that the meeting with Daniel Chapo represents "a new stage in the rapprochement between Washington and Maputo," in a context in which the United States is seeking to strengthen partnerships with politically stable African countries with relevant economic potential.

a3006.speaker: Sources in the Mozambican delegation (anonymous)
a3006.speech: Said the President underlined the need for international partners to invest not only in large-scale projects, but also in capacity-building initiatives, technological innovation and the training of young people.

a3102.speaker: Dr Lassana Sissoko, chief medical officer of the Kolondièba health district
a3102.speech: Presented a positive assessment, declaring: “Thanks to the efforts of the actors involved and the support of financial partners, health care provision improved in 2024.” Among the notable advances, he noted that contraceptive prevalence rose from 15% in 2023 to 20% in 2024, immunisation indicators for child survival were strengthened, seasonal malaria chemoprevention reached 100% across the four rounds (one of the best rates in Mali), and ANC4 coverage reached 36%, the best performance in the Sikasso Health Region.

a3102.speaker: Dr Lassana Sissoko, chief medical officer of the Kolondièba health district
a3102.speech: Announced ambitious objectives: “In 2026, we will strengthen the monitoring of essential community care (SEC) and the integration of services in health facilities.”

a3102.speaker: Amadou Dembélé, head of the local women’s promotion service
a3102.speech: Hailed the commitment of partners such as USAID, Kènya Sinsinwalle, the DTCs, the AECs, social development, CAFO and the youth, who “played a key role in our successes.”

a3224.speaker: Darius Dillon, Montserrado County Senator
a3224.speech: Rightly noted, "members of the House of Representatives have the rights and legal powers to remove a Speaker ... but for 'cause,' after 'due process of law.'" ; emphasized that bribery is a felony, and both the "giver and recipient" must be held accountable.

a3224.speaker: Rep. Luther Collins, Liberian House of Representatives member (testimony)
a3224.speech: Admitted to accepting US$15,000 to support Koffa's removal.

a3224.speaker: Congress for Democratic Change (CDC)
a3224.speech: The CDC's claim that the plan to oust the Speaker originated from the ruling Unity Party, whose Vice Standard Bearer, now Vice President of Liberia Jeremiah Koung, is a prime contender for the presidency in 2029.

a3224.speaker: Unnamed sources
a3224.speech: Some sources suggest that certain members of the Congress for Democratic Change (CDC) fear Koffa's potential rise as a presidential candidate in 2029.

a3224.speaker: Liberian lawmakers
a3224.speech: Lawmakers claimed the recent US$20 million "budget tampering" scandal was perpetrated by the Boakai administration.

a3314.speaker: Donald Trump, President of the United States
a3314.speech: Has ordered a halt to the distribution of drugs for AIDS, malaria and tuberculosis to countries that receive aid through the United States Agency for International Development (USAID); the order, issued on January 28, 2025, is aimed at reviewing various aid projects. His step also includes an order to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) to halt its cooperation with the World Health Organization (WHO).

a3314.speaker: International sources (duru za kimataifa)
a3314.speech: According to international sources, the order is expected to affect millions of people who depend on medical services through programmes such as the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR).

a3314.speaker: Aid-providing organisations, including Chemonics
a3314.speech: Have said the move will disrupt the availability of medicines and services for the most at-risk people.

a3314.speaker: Health experts
a3314.speech: Have warned that the decision could cause a new outbreak of diseases, with the drugs that prevent HIV transmission to 6.5 million children in 23 countries at risk of becoming unavailable ; experts say the decision will affect the fight against the threat of global diseases such as bird flu, the Marburg virus and the Mpox outbreak.

a3314.speaker: Aid organisations
a3314.speech: Have described the move as outright devastation for people who depend on international assistance from the United States.

a3433.speaker: Samuel Ogbuku's Primary 5 teacher
a3433.speech: "Why are you making so much noise? Don't you know you're the leaders of tomorrow? Leaders don't make noise. And you shouldn't."

a3433.speaker: Samuel Ogbuku, Managing Director/CEO of the Niger Delta Development Commission (NDDC)
a3433.speech: "Those words sank deep into my heart and became the rudder that has influenced my actions ever since. I took that tomorrow literally. I believed the next day was the tomorrow, my teacher was talking about. I began to look forward to every new day with great expectation, day after day, month after month and year after year until it became part of me to wait for that tomorrow to come." ; "Finally, I saw my dreams of becoming a leader come true because it was only leaders who graced the front pages of a newspaper."

a3433.speaker: World Bank (1995 report, cited by Samuel Ogbuku)
a3433.speech: Described the Niger Delta "as the least developed area of Nigeria, with per capita income of less than $280 per annum," adding that "all indices of development such as education, health, sanitation, job creation, water and other physical infrastructure, were far below acceptable standards."

a3433.speaker: Samuel Ogbuku, Managing Director/CEO of the NDDC
a3433.speech: Explained the "Rewind to Rebirth" agenda: "That realisation became the seed of the Rewind to Rebirth agenda of the Governing Board. The rewind part is essential because to move forward, we needed to look backward. What did the Commission do right? What went wrong and why? ... To rewind meant to go back to the core values on which the Commission was founded: equity, accountability, regional development. With rebirth we are saying that it is not enough to just critique the past. We must become something new. Something better. Rebirth speaks to our future. A reborn NDDC would not just repackage old ideas. We must transform the way we do things: How we select projects, engage communities, manage funds, and evaluate and communicate our successes. Rebirth means transitioning from a Commission known for the number of contracts it awards, to one that constantly impact lives and drive socio-economic growth and progress."

a3433.speaker: Samuel Ogbuku, Managing Director/CEO of the NDDC
a3433.speech: Reported about 7,483 NDDC projects in the past 25 years, of which about 3,357 are roads and bridges, about 611 are renewable energy projects, while 3,427 are still ongoing; noted, regrettably, while speaking on the topic of dashed expectations, that an "NDDC project had come to mean something abandoned, halfdone, or poorly done," but said optimistically that the aim of the rewind to rebirth vision is not to return to the "many years of unplanned and mismanaged project execution."

a3433.speaker: Samuel Ogbuku, Managing Director/CEO of the NDDC
a3433.speech: On institutional instability: "[T]here was institutional fatigue. The NDDC had become a revolving door of leadership. In twenty-three years, the Commission had seen seventeen managing directors in different mutations. Most lasted just over a year. A few stayed only months. The result was a crisis of continuity. No leader had the time or space to implement a vision. Every new board began afresh. Every new managing director had to start from scratch." ; "Management instability is at the root of the performance of the Commission. In 25 years, we have had the unenviable record of not having any chief executive officer complete his term of four years... Each new leadership wants to start their own projects, build their legacy and because the NDDC Act rotates these position from state to state, the managing directors come under intense pressure from their states to start new projects there. And suddenly, they are kicked out, another person comes in and they abandoned all those projects and start their own and the cycle continues. That is the simple reason we have uncompleted NDDC project littering all over the place."

a3433.speaker: KPMG (international management consulting firm, report commissioned by the NDDC board)
a3433.speech: "NDDC has experienced frequent board dissolutions and Executive Management changes, causing governance instability. We noted that the Board has been reconstituted six (6) times between 2000 and 2023 and there have been eight (8) and seventeen (17) changes in the Chairperson and MD positions, respectively. The most recent Board was dissolved after only five (5) months in office. This is attributed to the absence of a formal, politically independent process for Board and Executive Management removal. This instability of leadership has led to disruptions in the continuity of strategic initiatives and long-term projects; strategic misalignment within the Commission, loss of valuable institutional knowledge and expertise, and loss of stakeholder confidence."

a3433.speaker: Ogaga Ifowodo, former Delta State representative on the NDDC governing board (in a private audience with President Muhammadu Buhari, 7 January 2019)
a3433.speech: "No doubt, Mr President, you are aware that NDDC is saddled with many problems, some institutional, some statutory, and some socio-political that prevent it from optimal delivery on its mandate, and so of winning a great number of friends in the restive Niger Delta. It is my humble opinion that in order for NDDC to deliver on its founding mission of ‘rapid and sustainable development of the Niger Delta to one that is economically prosperous, socially stable, ecologically regenerative and politically peaceful,’ it is critically important that it be restructured and refocussed on its mandate during your tenure, and that this will require a special presidential order to be executed within 24 months. Most, if not all, of the problems that bedevil NDDC and which have led to the dissolution of previous boards, thus causing very costly instability, can be traced to this need."

a3433.speaker: Joe Abah, then Director-General of the Bureau of Public Service Reforms
a3433.speech: Said that everything that can possibly be wrong in an institution was to be found in NDDC.

a3433.speaker: Samuel Ogbuku, Managing Director/CEO of the NDDC
a3433.speech: Reminded that "Today, most of the government presence you see in rural communities in the region are NDDC projects" and that they "are the only signs of government activities there."

a3433.speaker: President Bola Tinubu (directive, as reported by Samuel Ogbuku)
a3433.speech: At inauguration, instructed the board to complete all abandoned projects in the region, including roads, bridges, schools, and healthcare facilities; "This is also in line with the directive from Mr. President, who has instructed that all funds released to the NDDC must be tied to specific, transformational projects and must be executed by firms with demonstrated capacity to deliver."

a3433.speaker: Samuel Ogbuku, Managing Director/CEO of the NDDC
a3433.speech: On federal backing: "At inauguration, Mr President directed us to complete all abandoned projects in the region, including roads, bridges, schools, and healthcare facilities. In our 2024 budget, Mr. President also approved for us to raise N1 trillion facility to finance the completion of some of our legacy projects that had been abandoned. The President has given us all the necessary support." He adds that, "Since the beginning of this administration, the statutory allocation to the Commission from the federal government has tripled."

a3433.speaker: Samuel Ogbuku, Managing Director/CEO of the NDDC
a3433.speech: States that the 27-kilometre Ogbia-Nembe Road constructed in partnership with Shell Petroleum Development Company is "the most outstanding partnership which NDDC has entered into since its inception"; reported that at the PPP summit in Lagos, NDDC "signed a memorandum of understanding with a United States-based firm, Atlanta Global Resources Inc, to build a railway network that will connect the nine states of the Niger Delta region"; and that NDDC has signed MOUs with the Nigeria Liquified Natural Gas Limited (NLNG) for collaboration "on diverse fronts in the delivery of sustainable development projects," and with the World Health Organisation (WHO) "towards the goal of implementing a health insurance scheme for Niger Deltans," while the MOU with the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) for youth development is as good as "dead" following the dissolution of the agency.

a3433.speaker: Samuel Ogbuku, Managing Director/CEO of the NDDC
a3433.speech: Writes that in 2023 NDDC "introduced a youth development and empowerment scheme designed to create a comprehensive resource database for the youth population of the Niger Delta region. The scheme, known as Holistic Opportunities, Projects, and Engagement (HOPE), aims to provide a platform to empower the region's youths on a sustainable basis.... They are expected to register on the database to benefit from jobs created in areas such as agro-allied production, technology, and others."

a3433.speaker: Samuel Ogbuku, Managing Director/CEO of the NDDC
a3433.speech: On the performance bond with the EFCC: "To strengthen the emerging internal culture of accountability and prudence, we entered into a Performance Bond with the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission, EFCC. That partnership was historic. It was the first time in the Commission's history that an anti-corruption agency was embedded into our performance structure. This bond allowed the EFCC to independently monitor procurement processes, contract implementation, and budget performance. It was a bold step. It sent a clear message that today's NDDC is committed to doing things differently and is not afraid of scrutiny. In fact, we welcome scrutiny. I believe transparency is not a threat to good work; it is proof of it."

a3433.speaker: Samuel Ogbuku, Managing Director/CEO of the NDDC
a3433.speech: On the 2025 agenda: "One of our top priorities as a board is to focus on legacy projects — not token gestures or fragmented, piecemeal projects that make no meaningful difference in people's lives. The NDDC is an intervention agency, and our interventions must be strategic and impactful. We aim to execute infrastructure and development projects that will connect communities, improve lives, and stand the test of time... we have also identified a critical flaw in our budgeting approach. It is counterproductive to propose a ₦10 billion project and allocate only ₦1 billion per year. That effectively turns a one-year project into a decade-long affair. We intend to correct this. Our new approach will prioritise full project funding within a single budget cycle wherever possible. That way, we can start and complete key projects within a year, eliminate cost overruns, and increase the Commission's credibility." ; "We are in a hurry to deliver convincingly on the mandate of the Commission. Our transformation appetite is huge."

a3433.speaker: Samuel Ogbuku, Managing Director/CEO of the NDDC
a3433.speech: On political pressure and desilting contracts: "As a Federal Government agency, there's bound to be a lot of political pressure. While you cannot totally eliminate these pressures, we try to minimise them." ; "One thing that has actually bedevilled the Commission over the years is the issue of payment of desilting. Desilting represents up to 70 per cent of NDDC's current debt burden. Most of these desilting payments are fake and that is one thing people have used to defraud the NDDC... Under my watch, NDDC will not pay for desilting. We are not going to award new desilting contracts except where it is extremely necessary... This decision has put us under intense pressure... It is not easy to take such a decision, it could even cost us our jobs. But we are undeterred. We want to do the right thing for the region. If we keep paying for desilting, we will not have any funds left to invest in the development of the region. To continue to fund desilting is to invest in the underdevelopment of the region." ; while bemoaning that the expectations of the people of the Niger Delta far surpass available resources, he pointed out the attitude of politicians who see NDDC as "a cash cow to fund their ambitions instead of a vehicle to develop the Niger Delta."

a3433.speaker: Chiedu Ebie, Chairman of the NDDC governing board (foreword to 'Rethinking the Niger Delta')
a3433.speech: Says the book is "a manifesto of transformation."

a3481.speaker: Nigerian Exchange (NGX) data
a3481.speech: According to the latest data from the Nigerian Exchange (NGX), foreign investors had pulled 420.37 billion naira out of the Nigerian equities market in the first quarter of 2025, representing a 251% year-on-year increase in outflows compared to the 119.81 billion naira recorded in Q1 2024 ; the NGX reported 2.232 trillion naira in total transactions for Q1 2025, of which 814.05 billion naira (36.47%) came from foreign investors and 1.41798 trillion naira (63.53%) from domestic participants.

a3481.speaker: Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN)
